title: 3 Promises For The First Day Of School
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Michael Linsin recommends three explicit promises teachers should make to their class within the first twenty minutes of the school year: a promise to treat students with respect, defined concretely as never raising your voice, threatening, scolding, or using sarcasm; a promise to listen and address problems like bullying or teasing; and a promise to follow the classroom management plan exactly as written, framed entirely around how it protects students' right to learn. He argues these promises, delivered with boldness and sincerity, immediately eliminate the primary sources of student anxiety and set a teacher apart from prior experiences students may have had. Linsin also notes that publicly committing to these promises creates accountability pressure on the teacher, reinforcing their own consistency. The article closes by describing the promises as a statement of belief in oneself, in students, and in the transformational power of great teaching.
points: Three specific promises — respect, listening/protection, and faithful adherence to the classroom management plan — should be delivered boldly within the first twenty minutes of the school year.
The respect promise should be defined in concrete behavioral terms: never raising one's voice, threatening, scolding, or using sarcasm.
The management-plan promise should be framed entirely around how it protects students' right to learn and enjoy school, not as a rules announcement.
Publicly committing to these promises creates self-imposed accountability pressure that helps ensure the teacher's own follow-through.
Making and keeping these promises is presented as eliminating the three primary causes of student anxiety and misbehavior at the start of the year.
quotes: Of the many items on your first-day-of-school checklist, three promises should go at the very top.
The promises should be delivered with boldness and sincerity and within the first 20 minutes of meeting your new class.
Depending on your grade level, it may include how you’ll never raise your voice in anger or how you’ll never threaten, scold, or manipulate or how you’ll never use sarcasm or cut down to size.
This is the ultimate promise that protects their right to learn and enjoy school. Thus, you must frame everything you say about why you’re so faithful to it in these terms.
You also put yourself on record—and your reputation on the line—which exerts just enough pressure to ensure your consistent follow through.
The promises are a statement of belief—in yourself, in them, and in the transformational power of great teaching.
